analysis.one_liner: Taxes publicly traded asset-management partnerships as corporations instead of partnerships.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill by the Senate's top tax writers that would have taxed asset-management partnerships like corporations died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Big investment firms that manage other people's money — such as private equity and hedge fund managers — are generally taxed like partnerships rather than corporations, so their earnings avoid the corporate income tax at the entity level. This bill would strip that partnership treatment from publicly traded firms whose income comes from investment advice or asset management, taxing them as corporations instead. Existing firms already traded or registered with the SEC when the bill was introduced would get a five-year transition, keeping the old treatment through mid-2012.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would gain a more even tax code and additional federal revenue, plus businesses that do not use the publicly traded partnership structure and currently compete against firms with the lighter tax treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Publicly traded partnerships that directly or indirectly derive income from investment adviser or asset management services would be taxed as corporations under Internal Revenue Code section 7704, rather than as partnerships.
The change would apply to partnership tax years beginning on or after June 14, 2007, so firms taking advantage of the structure going forward would be taxed under the new rules immediately.
Federal revenue would rise because income taxed as a partnership passes through without entity-level corporate tax, while income taxed as a corporation is subject to the corporate income tax.

Businesses outside the asset-management sector would compete on a more even footing, since the partnership exception had effectively let publicly traded investment firms avoid entity-level corporate tax that other public companies pay.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity firms, hedge funds, and other asset managers organized as publicly traded partnerships, which would owe entity-level corporate tax on their management income; their investors would bear some of this through lower returns. Existing publicly traded or SEC-registered firms would get a grace period until tax years beginning on or after June 14, 2012.

drawbacks.text: The five-year transition for partnerships already traded or registered on June 14, 2007 would delay most of the revenue effect to 2012 and give incumbent firms a five-year head start over new entrants.

The bill reaches partnerships that only 'indirectly' derive income from investment advice or asset management, which could pull in firms beyond the asset managers it was aimed at and create compliance disputes.

A good-faith objection to taxing these firms as corporations is that it subjects their earnings to the corporate tax on top of taxes investors already pay, which defenders of the partnership structure argue is double taxation that other businesses avoid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a targeted fairness fix: it removes an entity-level tax advantage available almost exclusively to publicly traded asset managers, and the five-year transition blunts the main disruption for existing firms. The costs fall almost entirely on a narrow, wealthy industry, though the double-taxation objection is a legitimate point of debate about corporate tax design more broadly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 14, 2007 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus introduced the bill on June 14, 2007, on behalf of himself and Sen. Chuck Grassley, the chairman and ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
Four senators cosponsored the bill — one Republican and three Democrats.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record after the referral, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded private equity, hedge fund, and asset management firms kept the lighter partnership tax treatment for the rest of the Congress and beyond, since no competing bill to tax these partnerships as corporations became law. Ordinary taxpayers gained nothing.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on June 14, 2007 and took no further action; no markup or vote ever occurred.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Asset managers using the publicly traded partnership structure
against.what_they_did: Fought efforts during 2007 to tax publicly traded asset-management partnerships as corporations, mounting a well-documented lobbying campaign as firms like Blackstone went public under the structure.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by the Democratic Finance chairman and the committee's top Republican, and its four cosponsors split 1 Republican and 3 Democrats; opposition to the bill came from the industry, not from a party bloc in any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers (publicly traded partnerships)
industries.note: The bill removes their ability to organize as publicly traded partnerships and thereby avoid entity-level corporate tax, subjecting their management income to the corporate tax. The industry's interest in keeping the lighter treatment runs against the public's interest in a tax code that taxes similar public companies similarly.

Asset managers' access to the partnership structure helped fuel a wave of IPOs of management firms in 2007; taxing them as corporations would have reduced the appeal of those listings and the underwriting fees that come with them.
Taxing publicly traded asset-management partnerships as corporations would raise federal revenue and narrow a tax advantage available to a narrow group of wealthy fund managers.
